summary: This script automates a build process that bundles and minifies web assets (CSS, JavaScript, etc.) defined in a YAML configuration file. It reads bundle definitions from manifest.yaml, concatenates input files for each bundle, minifies them using a Docker container, and writes the results to output files while tracking whether any errors occurred.

explanations.4: The `command -v yq` checks if the yq program exists and is accessible; the `&> /dev/null` redirects both standard output and errors to nowhere (silencing any output), so we only care about the exit code.
explanations.9: This sets a variable to the filename where bundle definitions are stored—similar to how you'd store config data.
explanations.14: This flag variable starts at 0 and will be set to 1 if any bundle fails, so we can report the final status at the end.
explanations.20: The `-r` flag tells yq to return raw output (plain text) instead of JSON-formatted output with quotes; `| length` counts how many bundles exist in the config file.
explanations.22: This is a C-style for loop; it runs from i=0 up to (but not including) bundle_count, incrementing i by 1 each iteration.
explanations.24: We're extracting the name of the bundle at index i from the YAML file; the `-r` flag ensures we get plain text without surrounding quotes.
explanations.30: We create a temporary filename that includes the file type (like css or js) so we know what kind of file we're building.
explanations.38: The `-f` test checks if the file exists and is a regular file (not a directory); if true, we append its contents to our temporary bundle file.
explanations.49: This ensures the directory path for the output file exists before we try to write to it; `dirname` extracts just the folder part of a file path.
explanations.51: We run a Docker container with the current directory mounted as `/src` inside the container, passing our temp file to the minifier tool inside that container.
explanations.58: When minification fails, we set the flag to 1 but continue processing other bundles instead of stopping immediately.
explanations.66: We check if the flag is still 1, meaning at least one bundle failed; if so, we print an error message to standard error (that's what `>&2` does) and exit with code 1.
